newsitem.title: UK: UK windfall tax unlikely to push up prices - IFS.
newsitem.headline: UK windfall tax unlikely to push up prices - IFS.

text.p: A planned windfall tax on the profits of Britain's privatised utility companies is unlikely to have much impact on their prices and investment, the Institute for Fiscal Studies said.

"Provided there is no doubt that the windfall levy will be imposed once and only once, and provided the tax base chosen is one that cannot be manipulated by changes to company behaviour, the windfall is likely to have only a limited impact on both prices and investment," it said in its "Green Budget".
"It is this presumption that the windfall tax will not be shifted on to current or future customers that underpins our conclusion that most of the windfall tax will be borne by shareholders."
The IFS said the windfall tax was an arbitrary measure that was difficult to reconcile with any principles of equity in taxation.
The choice of the tax base for the windfall tax would be of considerable importance to individual companies and their current shareholders.

It gave estimates of how a five billion stg levy might be distributed on four different bases -- company size, excess shareholder returns to December 1992, excess returns to December 1995 and excess pre-tax profits to December 1995.

"For example, the water companies would pay 570 million stg of the levy if it were based on a simple measure of firm size, such as total sales in a particular year, but almost three times that amount (1.4 billion stg) if it were based on a measure of excess shareholder returns from privatisation up to December 1995," the IFS said.
The institute concluded that a tax based on shareholder returns would appear most likely given the Labour party's justifications for a windfall levy.
"Legal advice seems likely to outweight any economic considerations on the choice of the tax base, since the government will undoubtedly be looking for a levy that is legally watertight," it added.
